claim: Plasmodium falciparum transmission has decreased substantially in Southeast Asia and the Greater Mekong Sub-region over the last two decades.
source: In Southeast Asia, and particularly the Greater Mekong Sub-region (GMS), Plasmodium falciparum transmission has decreased substantially over the last two decades (World Health Organization, 2011; World Health Organization, 2010b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to World Health Organization reports from 2011 and 2010b.

claim: All GMS countries have committed to ambitious malaria elimination timelines.
source: In Southeast Asia, and particularly the Greater Mekong Sub-region (GMS), Plasmodium falciparum transmission has decreased substantially over the last two decades (World Health Organization, 2011; World Health Organization, 2010b), setting the stage for pre-elimination scenarios, with all GMS countries committing to ambitious elimination timelines (World Health Organization, 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a World Health Organization report from 2013a.

claim: Spreading artemisinin resistance creates a race against time before malaria becomes untreatable with currently available drugs.
source: Alignment of global funding bodies' goodwill with sound national malaria control programmes is crucial for elimination timelines to be met (World Health Organization, 2013c; Alonso and Tanner, 2013), but spreading artemisinin resistance creates a race against time before malaria becomes untreatable with currently available drugs (World Health Organization, 2010a; World Health Organization, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to World Health Organization reports from 2010a and 2013b.

claim: Vector control and early diagnosis followed by effective antimalarial treatment have been the mainstay of malaria control programmes.
source: Vector control and early diagnosis followed by effective antimalarial treatment have been the mainstay of malaria control programmes
evidence: This is a statement of established practice in malaria control.

claim: Modelling based projections indicate that vector control and early diagnosis with treatment alone are unlikely to achieve P. falciparum malaria elimination before failing drug efficacy becomes an issue.
source: Vector control and early diagnosis followed by effective antimalarial treatment have been the mainstay of malaria control programmes, but modelling based projections indicate these approaches alone are unlikely to achieve P. falciparum malaria elimination before failing drug efficacy becomes an issue.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from modeling studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: The most abundant vector species in the GMS are exophilic, do not preferentially bite humans, and can bite quite early in the evening.
source: The most abundant vector species in the GMS are exophilic (mainly bite outdoors), do not preferentially bite humans, and can bite quite early in the evening (Sinka et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sinka et al., 2011.

claim: The bionomics of GMS vector species render typical vector control measures such as ITNs and IRS sub-optimal.
source: The most abundant vector species in the GMS are exophilic (mainly bite outdoors), do not preferentially bite humans, and can bite quite early in the evening (Sinka et al., 2011), rendering typical vector control measures such as insecticide treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS) sub-optimal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited vector behavior characteristics.

claim: Population wide interventions, including mass drug administration (MDA), are under consideration to clear the infectious reservoir in asymptomatic populations.
source: Population wide interventions, including mass drug administration (MDA), are under consideration to clear the infectious reservoir in asymptomatic populations and potentially hasten progress toward elimination (Poirot et al., 2013; World Health Organization, 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Poirot et al., 2013 and World Health Organization, 2015a.

claim: The proportion of the target population receiving mass interventions ('coverage') is believed to determine their success.
source: The proportion of the target population receiving these interventions ('coverage') is believed to determine their success (World Health Organization, 2013c; Slater et al., 2015; Okell, 2015; Stuckey et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including World Health Organization, 2013c; Slater et al., 2015; Okell, 2015; Stuckey et al., 2016.

claim: Malaria elimination campaigns have been carried out successfully in some countries or locally in specific regions.
source: Whilst malaria elimination campaigns have been carried out successfully in some countries or locally in specific regions (Snow et al., 2013; John et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2015b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Snow et al., 2013; John et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2015b.

claim: Reintroductions of malaria from surrounding endemic areas are a constant threat to elimination efforts.
source: Whilst malaria elimination campaigns have been carried out successfully in some countries or locally in specific regions (Snow et al., 2013; John et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2015b), reintroductions of malaria from surrounding endemic areas are a constant threat (Cohen et al., 2012; Galappaththy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2012; Galappaththy et al., 2013.

claim: The importance of mobile populations as a source of malaria transmission in the GMS has been emphasized in recent years.
source: The importance of mobile populations as a source of malaria transmission in the GMS has been emphasized in recent years (Pindolia et al., 2012; Prosper et al., 2012; Pindolia et al., 2014; Smith and Whittaker, 2014; Edwards et al., 2015; Guyant et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Pindolia et al., 2012; Prosper et al., 2012; Pindolia et al., 2014; Smith and Whittaker, 2014; Edwards et al., 2015; Guyant et al., 2015.

claim: Prompt treatment of new clinical cases through village malaria worker (VMW) or village health worker (VHW) networks has proven to be an effective case management strategy.
source: Prompt treatment of new clinical cases through village malaria worker (VMW) or village health worker (VHW) networks has proven to be an effective case management strategy (Maude et al., 2014; Rutta et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maude et al., 2014; Rutta et al., 2012.

claim: The way in which mass interventions are deployed determines their success likelihood.
source: We argue that the way in which mass interventions are deployed is what determines their success likelihood.
evidence: This is the central argument of the paper, to be supported by the modeling results.

claim: The most efficient and effective roll-outs are laid on a solid community engagement foundation, thus ensuring subsequent adherence and coverage, while preventing malaria reintroduction from adjacent areas.
source: The most efficient and effective roll-outs are laid on a solid community engagement foundation, thus ensuring subsequent adherence and coverage, while preventing malaria reintroduction from adjacent areas.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge of public health interventions.

claim: The model presented is an individual based, spatially explicit model of P. falciparum malaria transmission that includes all the programmatic implementation details of mass drug administration campaigns.
source: Here, we present an individual based, spatially explicit model of P. falciparum malaria transmission that includes all the programmatic implementation details of mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns.
evidence: This describes the model developed in the study.

claim: The impact of MDA campaigns is determined by the interaction between implementation logistics, patterns of human mobility and how transmission risk is distributed over space.
source: We uncover how the impact of MDA campaigns is determined by the interaction between implementation logistics, patterns of human mobility and how transmission risk is distributed over space.
evidence: This is a key finding from the modeling study.

claim: Malaria elimination is only realistically achievable in settings with very low prevalence.
source: Our results indicate that malaria elimination is only realistically achievable in settings with very low prevalence
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Malaria elimination can be hindered by spatial heterogeneities in risk.
source: Our results indicate that malaria elimination is only realistically achievable in settings with very low prevalence and can be hindered by spatial heterogeneities in risk.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: In highly mobile populations, accelerating MDA implementation increases likelihood of elimination.
source: In highly mobile populations, accelerating MDA implementation increases likelihood of elimination
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: If populations are more static, deploying less teams would be cost optimal.
source: if populations are more static, deploying less teams would be cost optimal.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Mass drug interventions can be an invaluable tool towards malaria elimination in low endemicity areas, specifically when paired with effective vector control.
source: We conclude that mass drug interventions can be an invaluable tool towards malaria elimination in low endemicity areas, specifically when paired with effective vector control.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on modeling results.

claim: The number of MDA campaigns and the initial mean prevalence across all villages are critical covariates when predicting MDA outcome.
source: Clearly, the number of MDA campaigns and the initial mean prevalence across all villages are critical covariates when predicting MDA outcome.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distributions characterizing how malaria risk is distributed over space are quite important for MDA outcomes.
source: The distributions characterizing how malaria risk is distributed over space also seem quite important.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Artemisinin resistance spread is very sensitive to the number of MDA campaigns, initial mean prevalence, number of intervention teams, and intensity of human population mobility.
source: Artemisinin resistance spread is very sensitive to those same covariates as well as to the number of intervention teams and the intensity of human population mobility (Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: There is an intricate relationship between the optimal timing of MDA campaign start, its implementation logistics, and malaria seasonality patterns.
source: We found that there is an intricate relationship between the optimal timing of MDA campaign start, its implementation logistics, and malaria seasonality patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: Deploying a higher number of MDA teams will yield a higher likelihood of reaching malaria elimination within 2 years, only when population mobility is high.
source: Deploying a higher number of MDA teams will yield a higher likelihood of reaching malaria elimination within 2 years, only when population mobility is high – Figure 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Using a smaller number of intervention teams is predicted to be advantageous in a population of lower mobility, especially when there is only one annual transmission peak and when the MDA start is delayed to day 60.
source: Using a smaller number of intervention teams is predicted to be advantageous in a population of lower mobility, especially when there is only one annual transmission peak and when the MDA start is delayed to day 60 (instead of the default start at the beginning of the calendar year).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: In settings with 2 malaria seasons per year, the first transmission peak occurs earlier in the year, making the faster 400 team implementation a better option in general.
source: In settings with 2 malaria seasons per year, the first transmission peak occurs earlier in the year, making the faster 400 team implementation a better option in general.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: Overall, a slower implementation is preferable, especially for the single peak seasonal profiles.
source: We should note that overall, a slower implementation is preferable, especially for the single peak seasonal profiles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the two peak scenarios, a higher number of teams would be beneficial as prevalence increases from 1%.
source: For the two peak scenarios, a higher number of teams would be beneficial as prevalence increases from 1%.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: Different transmission heterogeneity distributions incur quite different prospects for elimination.
source: When addressing how to maximize the chances of reaching elimination within a short time span by implementing an MDA strategy, we found that different transmission heterogeneity distributions (depicted in Figure 1D) incur quite different prospects – Figure 4 (Normal), Figure 4—figure supplement 1 (Log-Normal), and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 (Pareto).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figures 4 and supplements.

claim: The likelihood of reaching elimination is strikingly different when comparing the Pareto distribution with the other two distributions (Normal and Log-Normal), except when an extremely efficient vector control program is carried out for a couple of years.
source: The likelihood of reaching elimination is strikingly different when comparing the Pareto distribution (most skewed) with the other two (Normal and Log-Normal distributions), except when an extremely efficient vector control program is carried out for a couple of years.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: Coupling vector control with an MDA campaign vastly improves the chances for elimination across the low prevalence settings explored.
source: Coupling vector control with an MDA campaign vastly improves the chances for elimination across the low prevalence settings explored here
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The longer vector control can be sustained the more likely elimination becomes.
source: Coupling vector control with an MDA campaign vastly improves the chances for elimination across the low prevalence settings explored here, and the longer vector control can be sustained the more likely elimination becomes.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: There is a correlation between population mobility and number of MDA teams, with faster MDA implementations being preferred when the human population is more mobile.
source: Once again, there seems to be a correlation between population mobility and number of MDA teams, with faster MDA implementations being preferred when the human population is more mobile – Figure 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: More MDA rounds translate into higher likelihoods of malaria elimination.
source: We have demonstrated that more MDA rounds translate into higher likelihoods of malaria elimination
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: Resistance is very likely to increase dramatically if elimination is not achieved.
source: We have demonstrated that more MDA rounds translate into higher likelihoods of malaria elimination but also show how resistance is very likely to increase dramatically if elimination is not achieved.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The model was calibrated to the relationship between entomological inoculation rate (EIR) and falciparum malaria prevalence measured by microscopy.
source: The second calibration performed was to the relationship between entomological inoculation rate (EIR) and falciparum malaria prevalence. The data shows a non-linear relationship between EIR and Pf prevalence measured by microscopy (Guerra et al., 2007) in over 90 endemic countries
evidence: This describes a model calibration procedure using published data.

claim: The Pareto distribution for vector density across villages replicates the observed prevalence variance for a fixed EIR value much better than the Gaussian equivalent.
source: Note that the Pareto distribution for vector density across villages (blue dots) replicates the observed prevalence variance for a fixed EIR value much better than the Gaussian equivalent (red dots).
evidence: This is an observation from the model calibration shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The model was calibrated to the relationship between Pf prevalence and clinical case incidence using data from SE-Asian settings.
source: The third calibration assessed the relationship between Pf prevalence and clinical case incidence. This calibration is done to the subset of SE-Asian datapoints contained in the dataset published in Patil et al. (2009)
evidence: This describes a model calibration procedure using published data.

claim: The model assumes that asymptomatic and clinical infections are equally infective to mosquitoes throughout.
source: For simplicity, we have assumed that asymptomatic and clinical infections are equally infective to mosquitoes throughout.
evidence: This is a stated model assumption.

claim: Further empirical studies are greatly needed to better characterise the infectiousness of asymptomatic infections, which bears critical consequences for malaria elimination prospects.
source: In reality, further empirical studies are greatly needed to better characterise this controversial quantity that bears critical consequences for malaria elimination prospects (Aguas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about research needs, supported by a citation.

claim: Malaria elimination becomes more amenable if asymptomatic infections are less infectious.
source: In Figure 3—figure supplement 3 we demonstrate this critical nature, with malaria elimination becoming more amenable if asymptomatic infections are less infectious.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The true catalyst of malaria elimination is the crash of the infectious population of mosquitoes after MDA, rather than a complete elimination of infections in the human population.
source: We can then conclude that the true catalyst of malaria elimination is the crash of the infectious population of mosquitoes after MDA, rather than a complete elimination of infections in the human population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: The model presented predicts that an MDA's success likelihood is bounded by the initial malaria prevalence.
source: The model presented here predicts that an MDA's success likelihood is bounded by the initial malaria prevalence
evidence: This is a key finding from the modeling study.

claim: Very little attention has been paid to implementation logistics in MDA planning.
source: Although MDA is being revisited by the global community, very little attention has been paid to implementation logistics
evidence: This is an observation about current practice in the field.

claim: There seems to be no protocol adjustment across settings with completely different seasonality and human mobility patterns, risking a sub-optimal MDA outcome.
source: Although MDA is being revisited by the global community, very little attention has been paid to implementation logistics, and there seems to be no protocol adjustment across settings with completely different seasonality and human mobility patters, thus risking a sub-optimal MDA outcome.
evidence: This is an observation about current practice in the field.

claim: The model is an individual based, discrete time, spatially explicit, stochastic model, with explicit mosquito population dynamics and human population movements.
source: We developed an individual based, discrete time, spatially explicit, stochastic model, with mosquito population dynamics and human population movement.
evidence: This describes the model structure.

claim: The simulated synthetic population mimics the demographics of a set of 1000 villages in SE Asia.
source: The simulated synthetic population mimics the demographics of a set of 1000 villages in SE Asia
evidence: This describes the model population.

claim: The distribution of villages over space, village sizes and age distribution of people are likely not applicable to African settings.
source: The simulated synthetic population mimics the demographics of a set of 1000 villages in SE Asia, with the distribution of villages over space, village sizes and age distribution of people likely not applicable to African settings.
evidence: This is a limitation statement about the model's generalizability.

claim: Previously published models fail to explicitly model how interventions are carried out in the field.
source: Whilst previously published models are extremely good at representing the biological processes underlying malaria transmission, some even making very realistic assumptions on how coverage increases over time (Nikolov et al., 2016), they fail to explicitly model how these interventions are carried out in the field.
evidence: This is a critique of existing models, with a citation to Nikolov et al., 2016.

claim: In practice, teams of workers visit villages sequentially one by one, usually spending 4–7 days to deploy one MDA round in each village.
source: In practice, teams of workers visit villages sequentially one by one, usually spending 4–7 days to deploy one MDA round in each village
evidence: This describes real-world MDA implementation practices.

claim: The number of implementation teams is an input parameter in the simulation platform and each team behaves as an agent.
source: The number of implementation teams is then an input parameter in our simulation platform and each team behaves as an agent.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: Teams remain in each village for a fixed period of time (process = 4 days), assumed to be the time needed to complete one round of MDA per village.
source: They remain in each village for a fixed period of time (process = 4 days), assumed to be the time needed to complete one round of MDA per village
evidence: This describes a model parameter.

claim: The total number of days taken from start of first MDA round in the first village to end of first MDA round in the final village (D) depends on the number of implementing teams (Teams): D = V*process/Teams.
source: Given a total number of villages V, and a processing time process, the total number of days taken from start of first MDA round in the first village to end of first MDA round in the final village (D) depends on the number of implementing teams (Teams): D = V*process/Teams.
evidence: This is a mathematical relationship in the model.

claim: The model includes a flow diagram representing the natural history of Plasmodium falciparum infections in human populations.
source: Flow diagram representing the natural history of Plasmodium falciparum infections in human populations.
evidence: This refers to Figure 1A which shows the model structure.

claim: Uninfected individuals (S) can be infected at rate λ, with the probability of developing clinical symptoms (σ) depending on their immunity level i and number of lifetime infections j.
source: Uninfected individuals (S) can be infected at rate λ, with the probability of developing clinical symptoms (σ) depending on their immunity level i and number of lifetime infections j.
evidence: This describes the model structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Clinical infections (C) can be detected and subsequently treated at rate τ to a treated state (T), or naturally subside into an asymptomatic parasite carrier stage (A) at rate ε.
source: Clinical infections (C) can be detected and subsequently treated at rate τ to a treated state (T), or naturally subside into an asymptomatic parasite carrier stage (A) at rate ε.
evidence: This describes the model structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Treated individuals lose their drug at rate ω.
source: Treated individuals lose their drug at rate ω.
evidence: This describes the model structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: After recovery or treatment, individuals become susceptible with an added level of clinical immunity (Si+1).
source: After recovery or treatment, individuals become susceptible with an added level of clinical immunity (Si+1).
evidence: This describes the model structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Clinical immunity level decays at rate α.
source: Clinical immunity level decays at rate α.
evidence: This describes the model structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The probability of developing clinical malaria depends on individual's history of infection (cumulative number of infections) for each immunity level.
source: Probability of developing clinical malaria depending on individual's history of infection (cumulative number of infections) for each immunity level considered here.
evidence: This refers to Figure 1B which shows this relationship.

claim: The model includes a village connectivity network where geo-located villages appear as circles the size of which is proportional to the number of people living there.
source: Village connectivity network. Geo-located villages appear as circles the size of which is proportional to the number of people living there.
evidence: This refers to Figure 1C which shows the village network.

claim: Edge width in the village connectivity network reflects individuals' probability of travel between connected villages.
source: Edge width reflects individuals' probability of travel between connected villages.
evidence: This refers to Figure 1C which shows the village network.

claim: Each village is assigned a specific mosquito density/vectorial capacity, with transmission heterogeneity over space characterized by three different distributions.
source: Each village is assigned a specific mosquito density/vectorial capacity, with transmission heterogeneity over space characterized by three different distributions.
evidence: This refers to Figure 1D which shows the distributions.

claim: The model includes explicit mosquito population dynamics.
source: We developed a modular simulation platform that is customizable to any malaria transmission setting to provide realistic outcome predictions for local and global level interventions. The modules are the building blocks of an individual based, discrete time, spatially explicit, stochastic model, with explicit mosquito population dynamics and human population movements.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: The model includes human population movements.
source: We developed a modular simulation platform that is customizable to any malaria transmission setting to provide realistic outcome predictions for local and global level interventions. The modules are the building blocks of an individual based, discrete time, spatially explicit, stochastic model, with explicit mosquito population dynamics and human population movements.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: The model has villages with different mosquito densities connected by a human flow network, on which different interventions are deployed at different times.
source: We thus have villages with different mosquito densities connected by a human flow network, on which different interventions are deployed at different times (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the model structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: One particular innovation compared to previous published work is the inclusion of very detailed logistical processes related to intervention deployment in the field.
source: One particular innovation compared to previous published work (Gatton and Cheng, 2010; Okell et al., 2011; Maude et al., 2012; Gerardin et al., 2015; Nikolov et al., 2016) is the inclusion of very detailed logistical processes related to intervention deployment in the field.
evidence: This describes a novel feature of the model, with citations to previous work.

claim: The model was run 100 times for each parameter set when exploring factors driving MDA outcome prediction.
source: When exploring the factors driving MDA outcome prediction, we explored all possible combinations of parameter values presented in Table 1, comprising 3888 sets of parameters. The model was run 100 times for each parameter set.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: The model explored 3888 sets of parameters when investigating factors driving MDA outcome prediction.
source: When exploring the factors driving MDA outcome prediction, we explored all possible combinations of parameter values presented in Table 1, comprising 3888 sets of parameters.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: The model explored the layering of vector control interventions on top of a global MDA initiative with 3 ACT rounds.
source: We also explored the layering of further intervention efforts on top of a global MDA initiative (with 3 ACT rounds), such as the implementation of indoor residual spraying (IRS) or larvicidal deployment, for example.
evidence: This describes the simulation scenarios explored.

claim: Vector control effect size can be modelled as a reduction in vectorial capacity or EIR, as a direct consequence of a decrease in life expectancy, increase in sporogony cycle length and/or decreased biting rate on humans.
source: Vector control effect size can be modelled as a reduction in vectorial capacity or EIR, as a direct consequence of a decrease in life expectancy, increase in sporogony cycle length and/or decreased biting rate on humans.
evidence: This describes how vector control is modeled.

claim: A transmission reduction efficacy of 0.10 means that the implemented vector control strategy reduces the number of infectious bites per person per year by 10%.
source: Thus, a transmission reduction efficacy of 0.10 means that the implemented vector control strategy reduces the number of infectious bites per person per year by 10%.
evidence: This defines a model parameter.

claim: The model simulations evaluated the proportion of simulations in which elimination is reached for a range of vector control efficacy/duration of intervention pairs.
source: Thus, we ran simulations for a range of vector control efficacy/duration of intervention pairs and evaluated the proportion of simulations in which elimination is reached.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: The model includes three interconnected groups of agents: Villages, Humans and Mosquitoes.
source: The simulation model presented here is a multi-level agent-based model containing three interconnected groups of agents: Villages, Humans and Mosquitoes.
evidence: This describes the model structure.

claim: To calibrate model runs to a specific prevalence, the mosquito biting rate (beta) is varied whilst keeping all other parameters fixed.
source: To calibrate model runs to a specific prevalence we vary a free parameter beta [5], the mosquito biting rate, whilst keeping all other parameters fixed.
evidence: This describes the model calibration procedure.

claim: The model was run for 200 years to reach equilibrium during prevalence calibration runs.
source: To explore the effect of malaria interventions using dynamic transmission models, one usually assures that the model is run until an equilibrium is reached (thus establishing a control scenario), and then implements whatever the intervention of interest is.
evidence: This describes the model calibration procedure.

claim: The probability of a human agent being male is 0.48.
source: The probability of a human agent being male is ml [3].
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 0.48 given in Table 2.

claim: The age profile of human agents is sampled from a discrete distribution taken from Cambodian census data.
source: The age of a human is sampled from a discrete distribution specified by a vector of size maxage [4]. This vector is given by a csv file with maxage [4] integers, containing a discrete age profile taken from Cambodian census data.
evidence: This describes how age is assigned in the model.

claim: Each human agent is assigned an ITN with a probability of 0.5.
source: Each human agent is assigned with an ITN with a probability of netuse [8].
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 0.5 given in Table 2.

claim: Ownership of an ITN reduces the human agent's susceptibility/infectivity by 0.2.
source: Ownership of an ITN reduces the human agent's susceptibility/infectivity by itneffect [9].
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 0.2 given in Table 2.

claim: Three different distributions (Gaussian, Lognormal, Pareto) were explored to characterize how mosquito densities vary over space.
source: Given the lack of data to inform these distributions, we chose to explore three different ones (Mn, Ml, and Mp). Two of those distributions represent extreme scenarios: one in which all villages have approximately the same biting rate (Gaussian); another where the vast majority have very low biting rates with only a few hotspots (Pareto). The third distribution (Lognormal) illustrates an intermediate scenario
evidence: This describes the distributions explored in the model.

claim: The Gaussian distribution represents a scenario in which all villages have approximately the same biting rate.
source: Two of those distributions represent extreme scenarios: one in which all villages have approximately the same biting rate (Gaussian)
evidence: This describes one of the distributions used in the model.

claim: The Pareto distribution represents a scenario where the vast majority of villages have very low biting rates with only a few hotspots.
source: Two of those distributions represent extreme scenarios: one in which all villages have approximately the same biting rate (Gaussian); another where the vast majority have very low biting rates with only a few hotspots (Pareto).
evidence: This describes one of the distributions used in the model.

claim: The Lognormal distribution illustrates an intermediate scenario in which some villages have quite high transmission intensity, but where most have low mosquito abundance.
source: The third distribution (Lognormal) illustrates an intermediate scenario in which some villages have a quite high transmission intensity, but where most have low mosquito abundance.
evidence: This describes one of the distributions used in the model.

claim: The model chose not to create infectious mosquitoes during model set-up because mosquito infection prevalence reaches equilibrium in a matter of days.
source: For simplicity, we chose not to create infectious mosquitoes during model set-up. This is essentially due to the extremely fast timeframes of life events in mosquitoes compared to humans. The mosquito infection prevalence reaches equilibrium in a matter of days and thus its initialisation to non-zero values bears a negligible benefit.
evidence: This explains a modeling decision.

claim: Biting rates are calibrated for each combination of mobility, transmission distribution, and prevalence to ensure the system is at equilibrium.
source: We use a free parameter beta [5], the mosquito biting rate, to calibrate each simulation to the desired malaria prevalence. Biting rates are calibrated for each combination of mobility, transmission distribution, and prevalence to ensure the system is at equilibrium.
evidence: This describes the model calibration procedure.

claim: The model takes inputs from two CSV-formatted input files and a JSON-formatted configuration file.
source: The developed malaria micro-simulation platform takes inputs from two CSV-formatted input files and a JSON-formatted configuration file.
evidence: This describes the model's input structure.

claim: The two input files provide the model with a list of villages and a list of humans respectively.
source: The two input files provide the model with a list of villages and a list of humans respectively.
evidence: This describes the model's input structure.

claim: Model-wide and process-specific parameters are given by the configuration file.
source: Model-wide and process-specific, as opposed to agent-specific, parameters are given by the configuration file.
evidence: This describes the model's input structure.

claim: Time zero in the model is assumed to be the 1st of January 5 years prior to the first malaria post establishment/MDA initiation.
source: Once initialisation finishes, the main body of the model simulation starts. We assume time zero to be the 1st of January 5 years prior to the first malaria post establishment/MDA initiation.
evidence: This describes the model's temporal structure.

claim: For each individual and for every simulated daily time step, a uniform random number is drawn between 0 and 1 for each possible and valid transition process.
source: For each individual and for every simulated daily time step, a uniform random number is drawn between 0 and 1 for each possible and valid (according to the individual's status) transition process (e.g. whether the individual dies, is infected, is treated, etc) associated with that individual.
evidence: This describes the stochastic implementation of the model.

claim: The transition process occurs if and only if the number drawn is lower than its daily probability of occurrence.
source: The transition process occurs if and only if the number drawn is lower than its daily probability of occurrence.
evidence: This describes the stochastic implementation of the model.

claim: When a death event happens, a new infant agent is generated as a replacement and placed in the same village to keep population size constant.
source: When a death event happens, a new infant agent is generated as a replacement. The new agent is placed in the same village where the death took place to keep population size constant, and all its immunity and exposure related parameters reset.
evidence: This describes how the model maintains population size.

claim: Every human agent can display short-term mobility patterns, characterised by overnight stays in villages other than their home for a mean period of 3 days.
source: Every human agent can display short-term mobility patterns, characterised by overnight stays in villages other than their home for a mean period of ovstay [10] days.
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 3 given in Table 2.

claim: In a village with no malaria worker presence, treatment probability is reduced by a factor of 0.1.
source: In a village with no malaria worker presence, this treatment probability is reduced by nomp [15].
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 0.1 given in Table 2.

claim: The probability of a human agent with asymptomatic infection getting treatment is 10^-4.
source: The probability of a human agent with asymptomatic infection getting treatment is given by asymtreat [16].
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 10^-4 given in Table 2.

claim: In a village under MDA, the daily probability for a human agent to receive a round of ACT treatment is 1/1.5.
source: In a village under MDA, the daily probability for a human agent to receive a round of ACT treatment is tauab [17].
evidence: This is a model parameter with value 1/1.5 given in Table 2.
